🚨Google built an invisible watermark into every image Gemini has ever generated. Over 10 billion pieces of content marked.

That 10 billion figure covers multiple types of content. One engineer focused on images and used 200 samples to study the watermark.

SynthID is Google DeepMind’s watermark. In images, it’s designed to survive edits like cropping, compression and screenshots.

The engineer’s project, reverse-SynthID, found a recurring pattern in images from the same model.

> The pattern was strongest in the green color channel
> Its frequencies shifted with image resolution
> The detector reached a reported 90% accuracy

The project also reports weakening the watermark with little visible change to the image.

The engineer did it with signal processing, without access to Google’s code or systems.

note_tweet.text:
Can a language model learn what to forget while it reasons?

A paper called Neural Garbage Collection tests whether a model can manage its own KV cache, the working memory it uses to avoid redoing calculations for earlier tokens.

That cache grows as the model generates more reasoning steps. The researchers trained the model to pause periodically, decide which entries to drop, then continue with what it kept. 

The only training reward was whether it got the final answer right. The model learned how to reason and what to forget together, without examples telling it which entries to drop. 

On Countdown, AMC and AIME tasks, the model kept its peak cache at about one-third to one-half of the full size. It retained much of its accuracy and beat the other cache eviction methods tested.

note_tweet.text:
🚨 MIT proved you can delete 90% of a neural network without losing accuracy.

The “lottery ticket hypothesis” found that some networks contain smaller subnetworks that can match the original model’s accuracy.

These “winning tickets” can be trained from their original starting weights. The finding does not apply to every model.

The challenge was finding them.

The original method required training the full network first, then pruning it and retraining the remaining connections.

That extra work made the approach harder to use in production.

Hardware support offers another way to benefit from sparsity.

NVIDIA Ampere and newer GPUs support a specific 2:4 pattern, where two weights out of every four are zero.

Compatible operations can use less memory bandwidth and reach up to twice the compute throughput.

But 2:4 sparsity removes 50% of those weights, not 90%. It also does not guarantee twice the speed for an entire model or zero accuracy loss.

Training methods and software support help turn fewer weights into practical savings. Results still depend on the model, hardware and pruning pattern.

The lesson is promising: some networks can achieve similar accuracy with far fewer connections.

Finding those connections and running them efficiently remain separate challenges.
